one_liner: Source-available Rust XML stack with a libxml2-compatible C ABI; the vendor reports ~2.1x median DOM-parse throughput over libxml2.
what_it_does: SupXML is a from-scratch Rust reimplementation of the libxml2 feature set: a strict XML 1.0 parser, an arena DOM, XPath 1.0, XSD 1.0 with part of 1.1, XSLT, Schematron, RelaxNG, Canonical XML/Exc-C14N, recovery mode, and HTML5 through html5ever. The Rust API is its own (parse_bytes/parse_str return a Document, and XmlReader/XmlBytesReader are pull readers), not libxml2's. A separate, unpublished compat crate builds libsupxml2.so/.dylib with libxml2 symbol names and struct layouts. That library is the drop-in path for C callers and for bindings such as lxml and Nokogiri, once they are rebuilt against a system libxml2.
how_it_is_fast: The tokenizer is a strict byte-level SAX reader built on memchr SIMD searches. Text runs scan for '<', '&' and ']' in one memchr3 pass. A start tag jumps to the first '>' and accepts it if a memchr2 count of both quote characters before it is even; otherwise it falls back to a quote-aware scan. XML Name characters are checked against 256-entry ASCII lookup tables. XML 1.0 §2.2 character validation is one upfront SWAR pass over the whole document (the has-zero-byte trick, 8 bytes per iteration) instead of per-token checks, and UTF-8 is validated with simdutf8 (AVX2/SSE4.2/NEON dispatch). The DOM uses libxml2-shaped nodes allocated in one bumpalo arena per document, so each node costs a pointer bump and the whole arena is freed at once. Strings are borrowed from the owned source buffer where possible. An opt-in parse_bytes_in_place mode decodes entities inside the input buffer to avoid copies.
when_to_use: Rust services that need libxml2-class features (XSD 1.0 validation, XPath 1.0, XSLT, C14N for XML-DSig/SAML, recovery mode) without linking C, and that can get a Supso certificate: paid commercial, free 30-day evaluation, or free hobbyist for non-monetized projects

DOM-parsing UTF-8 documents from about 15 KB to 95 MB into an owned tree. The vendor's table shows 1.61x (pubmed) to 3.75x (Arabic gazali_maqasid_ar, 599 KB) over libxml2's xmlParseMemory; the largest gains are on text-heavy and non-ASCII documents

XSD pipelines with complex Microsoft-style particle and derivation schemas. On W3C XSTS 1.0, libxml2 goes quadratic and times out at 30 s on 3 schemas that SupXML compiles in under 1 ms, and total schema-compile time is 1.74 s vs 3.96 s
Browser or edge runtimes that need XML, XPath, XSLT, XSD or HTML parsing: it builds for wasm32-unknown-unknown with every feature except network-resolver
As a reference design for a strict, validating XML tokenizer built from memchr, SWAR and lookup tables
when_not_to_use: Any open-source, redistributable or unlicensed deployment. The LICENSE is proprietary Supported Source (not OSI), and every document-parse entry point returns a fatal error unless a valid certificate is found

Pure streaming or event workloads. The vendor's own page shows quick-xml faster on 4 of the 5 fixtures it lists (nasa 0.74x, swiss_prot 0.59x, wikipedia_ww2 0.11x), with only ~1.04x median across 21 fixtures at the matched contract
Maximum DOM speed on trusted input. Its own docs say parse_bytes_in_place with all four skip_* flags reaches 'roughly half of pugixml's throughput', and pugixml-beating siblings go further
HTML parsing for speed. It wraps html5ever and is at parity with libxml2 (~1.02x geomean on the docs page); COMPARISON.md even shows hn.html at 35 vs 45 MiB/s

Long-running processes that use the C-ABI shim on persistent threads, because per-document arenas are freed only at thread exit. Also note the maturity: 1 contributor, 1 GitHub star and 121 crates.io downloads

integration.form: crate (sup-xml on crates.io); C callers use a cdylib (libsupxml2.so/.dylib) built from the unpublished crates/compat with --features cdylib-exports
integration.dependencies: supso-project (offline Ed25519 + ML-DSA-44 license verification), memchr, simdutf8, bumpalo, rustc-hash, regex, chrono, rust_decimal, elsa, unicode-properties, log, encoding_rs (default full-encodings feature); optional: html5ever/markup5ever (html), ureq (network-resolver), bitflags (xsd)
integration.platforms: any Rust target; SIMD UTF-8 validation dispatches at runtime (AVX2/SSE4.2/NEON) with a scalar fallback; wasm32-unknown-unknown supported except the network-resolver feature
integration.thread_safety: Document is Send but not Sync. Parsing shares no mutable state, so any number of threads can parse concurrently. In the C shim each document gets its own arena, and the arena is kept alive until the thread exits.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — the Rust API is not libxml2's. The compat cdylib exports libxml2 symbol names and struct layouts, and the vendor reports lxml 47/47 and Nokogiri 17/17 operations identical after rebuilding those bindings against a system libxml2. Differences: Perl XML::LibXML's xmlTextReader usage is not yet covered, the entity-expansion cap is 1 MB vs libxml2's ~10 MB, recovery keeps a bare '&' where libxml2 drops the text, and node memory is freed only at thread exit. cdylib-exports is off by default because linking the shim and the real libxml2 into one binary causes undefined behavior (xmlFree shadowing).

gotchas: Runtime license gate: the first parse in a process looks for a certificate (SUPSO_LICENSE_PATH, ~/.supso/license_certificates/, ./.supso/license_certificates/). Without one, every parse returns a fatal error. An expired certificate only gets a logged grace period before parsing fails.

The headline benchmark is not symmetric. The timed sup-xml call is parse_bytes_unchecked, which skips encoding sniffing and SIMD UTF-8 validation (the harness checks UTF-8 outside the timer). It also runs with the default namespace_aware: false, so there is no xmlns scanning or QName resolution. libxml2's xmlParseMemory does detection and validation inside the timer and uses its namespace-aware SAX2 interface. Timing is best-of-N with no warmup (default N=2), and 'MB/s' is actually MiB/s.

The project's own documents disagree. COMPARISON.md gives ~1.0-1.3x median vs libxml2 against the docs page's ~2.1x. The README claims 255/257 on the W3C XML Conformance Suite, but the COMPARISON.md table shows 244/257. An XSD instance-validate time of 1.12 s vs 2.85 s is described as 'parity'. A bench comment still says gazali parses at ~14 MB/s vs libxml2's ~140 MB/s.

The defaults differ from libxml2: namespace_aware is false (set it true for prefixed XPath), there is a 1 MB entity-expansion cap and a depth limit of 256, and external DTDs are not loaded. The 'memory-safe' claim is scoped: unsafe code is allowed in the scanner, readers, parser, encoding and dom.rs, and the C shim is #![allow(unsafe_code)] even though CONTRIBUTING lists the shim among the forbid-unsafe modules.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Choose it over yxml, quick-xml, xmloxide or rusty_xml only when you need libxml2's broader surface (XSD, XSLT, XPath, C14N, recovery) in memory-safe Rust or behind a libxml2 C ABI, and you are willing to license it. For plain streaming, quick-xml beats it on most fixtures in SupXML's own table. yxml offers a similar ~2.2-2.4x over libxml2 in a tiny C SAX parser. xmloxide is the other pure-Rust libxml2 reimplementation, catalogued at roughly libxml2 parity.
verified_claims_summary: This is a first-party bench (cargo bench -p sup-xml-bench --bench head_to_head). It compares sup-xml's bumpalo-arena DOM (parse_bytes_unchecked, default options, input copied into an owned buffer) with libxml2 xmlParseMemory plus xmlFreeDoc through FFI, taking best-of-N MiB/s per fixture. The 11 fixtures shown range from 1.61x to 3.75x, the claimed median over 21 is ~2.1x, and the XSTS 1.0 wall-clock is 2.86 s vs 6.81 s with libxml2's 3 timeouts excluded. No CPU, OS, rustc version, flags or libxml2 version is disclosed; build.rs links whatever libxml2 pkg-config or the macOS system provides, and the numbers have not been independently reproduced.
status_note: The project is actively developed by a single maintainer (111 commits from one contributor; v1.3.0 released 2026-06-17; last commit 2026-06-20). It is reference-only here because the proprietary Supported Source license requires a paid or free-tier certificate, and parsing fails without one.
